summary: We built Red Dust Protocol, a browser-based Mars survival game that trains junior astronauts (ages 7–12). Isolated 225 million km from Earth, players must keep four astronauts alive for 30 sols across three difficulty modes. Instead of a textbook quiz, players manage six draining systems—Oxygen, Water, Food, Power, Morale, and Hull—with only four crew members while facing dust storms, solar flares, and airlock leaks. Every crisis pairs live NASA photos with science facts, helping kids learn through cause and effect how astronauts survive on Mars.
details:
What it does and how it works In Red Dust Protocol, your goal is to survive 30 sols on Mars across three difficulty modes (Cadet, Commander, and No Margin). The core challenge comes down to simple math: you have 6 habitat meters that drain every single day—Oxygen, Water, Food, Power, Morale, and Hull—but you only have 4 astronauts to assign to jobs. Because you can never staff all 6 stations at once, you have to read the "next sol" resource projections and rotate your crew before a minor shortage turns into an emergency.

We also built the systems to depend on each other just like a real habitat:

  • If Power drops below 25, the whole base browns out and every job runs at 60% efficiency.
  • If Morale drops below 25, tired astronauts work at 75% efficiency (and if both Power and Morale are low, efficiency drops to 45%).
  • If Hull drops below 30, micro-breaches leak an extra 4 Oxygen every sol.

At the end of a sol, random hazards can hit the base—like a global dust storm that cuts solar panel output to 40%, a meteor shower, a failed water pump, or a solar flare. Each crisis pops up with a real NASA photo, a short science fact, and a tough trade-off (for example, sending a crew member outside to wipe dust off the solar panels vs. sheltering and losing power for 4 sols).

Benefits and intended impact Most space games for younger students are either arcade shooters or disguised multiple-choice quizzes. We wanted 7–12 year olds to actually think like mission controllers. When a player loses a run because they ignored hull maintenance or let a dust storm drain their batteries, the end screen gives them a specific root-cause debrief (like Total Blackout or Dehydration) and compiles a log of all the NASA facts and links they unlocked during their mission. By the second or third try, players naturally understand why the ISS recycles 98% of its water and why Mars habitats need radiation shelters.

Tools, coding languages, and software used We built the entire project as a single, zero-dependency file (red-dust-protocol.html) using:

  • HTML5, CSS3, and Vanilla JavaScript for the state engine, turn loop, and UI.
  • NASA Image and Video Library REST API (images-api.nasa.gov) to dynamically fetch and credit real NASA photos matching the current sol’s briefing or active hazard.
  • Inline SVG & CSS Keyframe Animations for the 12 custom hazard scenes and the 4 time-of-day sky phases (Dawn, Midday, Dusk, Night).
  • Web Audio API to synthesize all 16 sound effects (rocket launches, alarms, airlock hisses, dust winds, and button clicks) directly in the browser using oscillators and noise buffers, without needing external MP3 files.

How it is creative & factors our team considered When designing the project, our biggest priority was accessibility for schools and students. Many classroom computers or home connections have slow internet or strict firewalls, so we designed a hybrid architecture: when online, the game pulls live NASA photography, but if a player is offline, it automatically falls back to our custom-coded SVG illustrations and synthesized Web Audio so the game never breaks. We also ran 2,000 automated bot simulations across all three difficulty levels to balance the daily drain numbers, making sure Cadet is forgiving for beginners while No Margin is a genuine survival puzzle.
